title: Path.exists() first checks whether a file or folder exists
body: Path.exists() returns True or False to indicate whether the specified path actually exists. Checking this before reading a file makes it easier to narrow down the cause of a FileNotFoundError.
detail: The `exists()` function checks whether a file or folder exists. Therefore, it’s a good habit to also use `is_file()` to verify that it’s a file, or `is_dir()` to verify that it’s a folder. Beginners should first verify that the path is correct and that the location is relative to the current working directory. If you’re confused about relative paths, try using `Path.cwd()` to display the current location.

title: is_file() and is_dir() distinguish between files and folders
body: Even if `exists()` returns `True`, you still need to check separately whether it is a file or a folder.
detail: `is_file()` is used to check if an item is a file, and `is_dir()` is used to check if it is a folder; this allows you to distinguish between reading a file and listing the contents of a folder. For example, even if a path named "data" exists, if "data" is a folder, you cannot read it directly using `read_text()`. Conversely, when creating an output folder, you must verify that it is a folder and not a file. By distinguishing between `exists()`, `is_file()`, and `is_dir()`, you can identify path errors more quickly.

title: mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) creates the necessary folders
body: mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) creates missing parent directories and continues when the same directory already exists. It still fails if the path is a regular file or permissions are insufficient.
detail: It does not suppress every error.

title: Before writing a file, prepare the parent folder.
body: The "parent" in a file path refers to the folder where the file will be placed. Calling `path.parent.mkdir(...)` before `write_text()` can help reduce save failures.
detail: For example, to write to `output/result.txt`, the `output` folder must exist first. `path.parent` points to the `output` folder, not to `result.txt` itself. That’s why storage pipelines often follow the sequence of creating the parent folder first and then writing the file. Separating the filename and folder name makes it easier to identify the cause of a storage failure.
